decisions.quote: To address frequent disruptions in an urban elementary lunchroom, McCurdy et al. (J Sch Psychol 47:39–54, 2009) developed a team-based interdependent group contingency called the Lunchroom Behavior Game (LBG) and observed decreased disruptions, while staff and students found the intervention highly acceptable. Given this success, we replicated the LBG in an elementary school in a mid-sized Southeastern city. LBG implementation was staggered across three lunch periods using a multiple-baseline design across subjects. The rate of disruptive behaviors decreased in all lunches following LBG implementation and remained at lower levels during maintenance observations; however, implementation fidelity and student acceptability were low.
decisions.reason: The supplied text states no overall replication verdict (Rule 1), so outcome is governed by Rule 2 and the codebook rule that a tested finding contrasted with the original may not be left out. The abstract explicitly identifies two findings from McCurdy et al. (2009)—decreased disruptions and high staff and student acceptability—and reports corresponding results that agree on decreased disruptive behaviors but explicitly contrast (; however,) low student acceptability, yielding mixed.

scope_review.parent_objection: Original abstract explicitly states McCurdy2009 decreased disruptions AND staff/students found intervention highly acceptable. Current study decreases disruptions BUT says implementation fidelity and student acceptability were low. First reply excludes acceptability as implementation issue around central effect. Exact codebook says robustness/exploratory analyses may be left out but a tested finding paper itself contrasts with original may not. Is student acceptability a directly compared original finding (mixed), or merely new implementation quality without an original test being replicated (successful)? Read complete supplied abstract and codebook; do not dismiss explicit original acceptability as incidental without source basis. No overall replication verdict states all results confirmed.

prior_reply.quote: To address frequent disruptions in an urban elementary lunchroom, McCurdy et al. (J Sch Psychol 47:39–54, 2009) developed a team-based interdependent group contingency called the Lunchroom Behavior Game (LBG) and observed decreased disruptions, while staff and students found the intervention highly acceptable. Given this success, we replicated the LBG in an elementary school in a mid-sized Southeastern city. LBG implementation was staggered across three lunch periods using a multiple-baseline design across subjects. The rate of disruptive behaviors decreased in all lunches following LBG implementation and remained at lower levels during maintenance observations; however, implementation fidelity and student acceptability were low. Specific implementation issues encountered and recommendations for future research are discussed.
prior_reply.reason: The central finding tested by the multiple-baseline single-case replication design—that implementing the Lunchroom Behavior Game reduces disruptive lunchroom behaviors—was replicated across all three lunch periods and maintained during maintenance observations. Low implementation fidelity and student acceptability are paired together as implementation issues around the intervention rather than a failed replication of the central behavioral effect.
